newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto says IMF accord by caretakers not binding.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto says IMF accord by caretakers not binding.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto said on Sunday any accord signed by the present caretaker government with the International Monetary Fund should not be binding for the next elected government.
"We demand that whatever agreement with the IMF, it should be front-loaded, that is it should be for now not for the coming government," she told a news conference.

The IMF said on Thursday it expected to reactivate and possibly expand a stalled $600 million standby loan to Pakistan next month and to start early discussions on a longer-term structural adjustment loan.

But Bhutto, who expressed confidence that her government ousted by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on charges of corruption and misrule would be restored by the Supreme Court, said the next government should have the freedom to take its own decisions.
"If we are restored within a month, we should be able to decide what we want and what not," she said.

The IMF said it had confirmed a draft agreement reached with Bhutto's ousted government on the basis of a stabilisation package announced on October 22, and expected the IMF board to approve the immediate release of two stalled tranches worth $160 million by the first half of December.
Bhutto said she did not believe caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid's government had reached an agreement with the IMF.

"The IMF also knows that this case (her sacking) has to go before the Supreme Court and it has yet to be decided whether this government survives or the Benazir government is restored, or elections will be held and a new government will be born."
Khalid's finance and economic affairs adviser Shahid Javed Burki plans to visit Washington in early December for talks with the IMF on a new extended structural adjustment facility.
Pakistan needs funds to replenish its depleted foreign reserves and make payments due next month on its foreign debt, which stood at $28.6 billion at the end of June.
The IMF withheld disbursements of a standby loan due in June and September because it was unhappy with the Bhutto government's economic performance and the budget for 1996/97.
